title: Easter Island was not ecological suicide: European plague killed the population, not forest deforestation
dek: Europeans landed four years before Captain Cook arrived, bringing Old World diseases to which islanders had no immunity; the real population destroyer was this plague, not forest deforestation caused by islanders themselves.
why: Worth listening to because evidence is verifiable: stone statue walking experiments, rat DNA, and quarry workshop distribution are all concrete evidence, not abstract conclusions.
who: People interested in prehistoric Pacific migration and archaeological methodology, especially readers wanting to know how legends and hard evidence cross-verify.
skip: 0:00–2:00 is advertising and opening pleasantries; can be skipped.

points.h: Settlement timing aligned with East Polynesian diaspora
points.body: Radiocarbon dating shows Rapa Nui settled around AD 1200, nearly simultaneous with Hawaii, slightly after the Marquesas, and before New Zealand. Terry Hunt notes that East Polynesian peoples discovered and colonized over a thousand Pacific islands within just one or two centuries, including Auckland Islands near Antarctica—an extraordinarily rapid expansion, not a slow gradual penetration.

points.h: Rat DNA suggests possibly only one founding canoe
points.body: Polynesian rat DNA on Rapa Nui is remarkably homogeneous, unlike Hawaii or New Zealand with multiple distinct lineages indicating multiple settlement waves. This suggests the island experienced just one colonization voyage; afterward, islanders never returned to East Polynesia because local palm wood was unsuitable for building ocean canoes, trapping them permanently on the island.

points.h: Stone-covered fields: innovation to fertilize impoverished volcanic soil
points.body: Rapa Nui's soil drains too quickly, losing nutrients rapidly. Islanders invented stone mulch and built manavai—walled garden enclosures that block wind and retain compost. Critically, young volcanic rock itself continuously leaches phosphorus and nitrogen into the soil, functioning as natural rock fertilizer. Satellite imagery identifies over 3,000 manavai across the island.

points.h: Thirty quarry workshops, not a chieftain's decree
points.body: Over 95% of moai came from Rano Raraku's tuff cone. Close study reveals roughly 30 independent workshops, each with space for only 10–15 workers. Evidence shows different communities claimed separate plots and carved their own statues rather than executing an island-wide project under centralized command—different regions' moai even show distinct facial styles.

points.h: Stone statues genuinely walked: rope, center of gravity, and 18 people
points.body: Oral tradition says statues ‘walked’ to their destinations. Terry Hunt's team built a 4.35-ton replica and discovered that transported moai lean forward with low centers of gravity—only elevated after reaching their platforms by removing stone from below. Using three ropes to rock a statue side-to-side, just 18 people made it ‘walk’ 100 meters in 40 minutes; the largest documented transported moai, about 80 tons, required only 50–60 people.

points.h: Building statues was inter-community rivalry, not unified effort
points.body: Transporting moai required no island-wide coordination—individual communities completed their own statues, then displayed them to neighbors. Hunt describes the mindset as nearly ‘see what we can do, dare you to move one, how much bigger will yours be next year?’—both cooperation and competition drove escalating statue size, with some red volcanic-stone topknots (pukao) weighing nearly 11 tons.

points.h: Rats, not logging, killed the forests
points.body: Polynesian rats brought by islanders faced no predators and found nearly infinite food in palm fruit, multiplying to millions within three years and constantly eating palm seeds, preventing forest regeneration. Combined with land-clearing for agriculture, forests gradually vanished over centuries. Yet Hunt emphasizes forest loss barely affected islanders' livelihood—palms actually blocked farmland, hardly an ecological suicide.

points.h: Cook arrived at a plague-ravaged island, not one ecologically collapsed
points.body: When Captain Cook arrived, population was sparse and skeletons lay scattered; he and naturalists aboard guessed some past disaster had struck, which later scholars blamed on deforestation-driven ecological collapse. But Spanish visitors four years earlier almost certainly brought Old World pathogens to which islanders had zero immunity. Hunt argues Cook witnessed not ecological ruin but the population collapse caused by that plague.
